Mode 3: the element has a thick border in the same color as the focus ring (e.g. a {border: medium solid b
scenario: Government civic-portal primary nav of 6 links, each given a permanent outline:1px dotted #000; the UA keyboard-focus ring (itself a 1px dotted black line) is left intact, so the focused link is visually identical to its five permanently-dotted neighbours (F78 mode 2).
mechanism: Every nav link has a resting outline:1px dotted #000 identical in style/weight/colour to the UA focus ring; on Tab the UA dotted ring is drawn but blends into the already-dotted siblings, so a sighted keyboard user cannot tell which link has focus though the pixel diff is non-zero.

aspectDescription: An indicator can satisfy the pixel-diff rule while remaining effectively invisible to a human. G195 sets concrete guidance for a genuinely visible author indicator: an area at least a 1 CSS px border around the component (or at least 4 CSS px along the shortest side), and a contrast change of 3:1 or more between focused and unfocused states (or, failing 3:1, at least 2px thick). A page can change SOME pixels with a 1px outline whose color barely differs from the background, a faint sub-3:1 box-shadow, or a fractional letter-spacing nudge that only shifts a few antialiased edge pixels — so the
scenario: Newspaper article/section-nav links whose only keyboard-focus change is the link text color shifting from #000000 to #0a0a0a on a white page (default outline removed). A real but sub-perceptual ink shift.
mechanism: The sole :focus change is a text-color move #000->#0a0a0a on #ffffff = a contrast CHANGE of ~1.06:1 (verified rendered maxChannelDelta=10/255). aspectTitle: Script removes or steals focus the instant an element receives it (F55: onfocus blur / programmatic focus theft)
aspectDescription: F55 is a failure where script removes focus the moment an element receives it (onfocus="this.blur()", or a handler that immediately moves focus elsewhere). Because focus never settles, no focus indicator is ever shown for that element, and the control becomes pointer-only. This is a temporal/behavioral failure: a single focused snapshot may even render as unfocused because focus has already been stolen. F55's test requires confirming that 'when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it' — a property over time, not a single render. The brief notes the corpus is st
scenario: Online-banking 'Move money' form whose 'Review transfer' submit button carries onfocus="this.blur()" (canonical F55 Example 1). Tabbing from the Memo field to the submit button lands focus and instantly removes it; the valid :focus outline never paints and the button is mouse-only. Junior dev pasted a Stack Overflow 'remove ugly focus ring' snippet.
mechanism: Inline onfocus="this.blur()" on input[type=submit]: the focus event fires and the handler calls .blur() in the same tick, so the declared .btn-primary:focus outline never renders. Verified by Puppeteer Tab traversal — focus moves Memo -> body -> Clear, never settling on 'Review transfer'.

aspectTitle: Visual feedback exists only for pointer interaction (:hover/:active) or is suppressed for keyboard (:focus-visible mismatch), leaving keyboard focus bare
aspectDescription: C15 and C45 stress that the visible feedback must apply to the KEYBOARD focus state, not only pointer interaction. A common real-world failure: authors write ':hover {…}' and ':active {…}' (or rely on JS mouseenter/mouseleave) but never ':focus'/':focus-visible', while also stripping the UA outline. A mouse user sees rich feedback; a keyboard user tabbing through gets nothing. The subtle, judgment-requiring variants are where this matters: :focus-visible heuristics that the UA suppresses for certain elements, :focus reused for both states but styled with mouse-targeted changes, or focus-within
scenario: Farm-to-table bistro primary navigation. Links light up with a pale-mint pill (#dcffff) on :hover/:active; the UA focus ring is removed via nav.primary a:focus{outline:none} with no replacement. A mouse user sees the pill; a keyboard user tabbing through the menu sees nothing change on the focused link. HEAD case (website-builder/marketing-template default).
mechanism: Visible feedback is bound exclusively to pointer-modality pseudo-classes (:hover and :active). Tab fires :focus, whose only declared rule is outline:none, so the keyboard-focused link is pixel-identical to its idle state. The link is still announced to screen readers, but the sighted keyboard user — the population 2.4.7 protects — has no indication of focus position.

scenario: Real-estate listings card grid. Each card (<article>) has a lift+shadow bound to .card:hover and .card:focus-within; the real focusable address <a> has outline:none. Tabbing onto a listing DOES lift the wrapper card, but the lift is on the wrong node, is pixel-identical to hover, and the focused link itself is bare. mechanism: Subtle present-but-wrong-node failure. On Tab, :focus-within fires and the wrapper lifts (transform:translateY(-3px) + shadow), so something visibly changes — but it marks the entire tile rather than the focused control (the link's own outline was removed), so with multiple cards visible the user cannot tell which element holds focus, and the change is indistinguishable from hover. A naive 'did anything change under programmatic focus?' pixel-diff (like oj04fd) would be fooled into passing.

The subtle, judgment-requiring variants are where this matters: :focus-visible heuristics that the UA suppresses for certain elements, :focus reused for both states but styled with mouse-targeted changes, or focus-within
scenario: E-commerce checkout shipping-country field built as an ARIA combobox with aria-activedescendant. The blue option highlight (.opt.hot) is toggled only by mousemove/mouseleave; the ArrowUp/ArrowDown handler updates aria-activedescendant (so screen readers announce the active country) but never paints the active option, and no CSS targets the active descendant. A sighted keyboard user arrowing the list sees nothing move. LONG-TAIL case (mouse-era autocomplete ported to ARIA).
mechanism: In an aria-activedescendant widget DOM focus stays on the input, so the visually-indicated active option IS the focus indicator the keyboard user needs. Here the highlight (.opt.hot) is bound to mousemove, a pointer event keyboard navigation cannot fire; the keydown handler moves aria-activedescendant but applies no class, and there is no [aria-activedescendant]-correlated CSS rule. The screen-reader user hears the active option; the sighted keyboard user sees the highlight frozen on whatever the mouse last touched, or nothing.

aspectTitle: Visual feedback exists only for pointer interaction (:hover/:active) or is suppressed for keyboard (:focus-visible mismatch), leaving keyboard focus bare
aspectDescription: C15 and C45 stress that the visible feedback must apply to the KEYBOARD focus state, not only pointer interaction. A common real-world failure: authors write ':hover {…}' and ':active {…}' (or rely on JS mouseenter/mouseleave) but never ':focus'/':focus-visible', while also stripping the UA outline. A mouse user sees rich feedback; a keyboard user tabbing through gets nothing. The subtle, judgment-requiring variants are where this matters: :focus-visible heuristics that the UA suppresses for certain elements, :focus reused for both states but styled with mouse-targeted changes, or focus-within
scenario: SaaS pricing page (Solo/Team/Business) with one CTA <button> per tier. The buttons define exactly one styled interactive state: .cta:active{transform:scale(.97)} (a press animation); .cta:focus is reset to outline:none with no replacement. Tabbing onto a CTA and pausing shows no change, because :active only fires while the button is held and springs back on release. MID case (Tailwind/utility-class mindset: focus:outline-none + active:scale-95).
mechanism: :active is the 'currently being activated' state, not a focus state. It fires for a mouse press and for keyboard Space/Enter activation but lasts only while the control is held and reverts instantly on release. With :focus reset to outline:none and no persistent replacement, a keyboard user who Tabs to a CTA and stops sees the button exactly as idle and cannot tell which of the three CTAs holds focus — violating the requirement that the indicator remain while focus is shown.

aspectTitle: Custom-drawn indicator that vanishes in forced-colors mode or that AT cannot track (G165 / C40 caveats)
aspectDescription: G165 warns that if you draw your OWN focus indicator (e.g. coloring sections of the page in response to user action) rather than using the native indicator, user/AT system-wide focus customizations 'will not carry over, and AT will not usually be able to find your focus indicator.' C40 adds the forced-colors caveat: relying on box-shadow alone fails because 'user agents commonly suppress the box-shadow property in forced-color modes.' So an indicator can look fine in the single default render oj04fd snapshots, yet disappear (box-shadow / background-image / gradient suppressed) or become orphan
scenario: Public-library 'Current loans' page whose primary 'Renew' buttons get their only focus indicator from a box-shadow glow applied after outline:none. HEAD case (Bootstrap/Tailwind-style 'remove ugly ring, add a nice glow' reset). Looks correct in the default render so oj04fd passes, but forced-colors/Windows High Contrast suppresses box-shadow, leaving no focus cue.

In forced-colors mode the UA suppresses the box-shadow property while outline:none still applies, so the focused button renders identically to unfocused ones — no focus indicator survives for forced-colors keyboard users before an irreversible 'Renew' action.

aspectTitle: Focus indicator drawn but clipped by overflow or pushed outside the visible viewport so the user never sees it
aspectDescription: The SC requires a perceptible focus indication for the focused element. A real-world failure: the element receives focus and an indicator IS drawn, but it is clipped by an ancestor's overflow:hidden, hidden behind a sticky/fixed header or off-canvas panel, or the focused element sits scrolled out of the visible viewport, so the changed pixels are never actually seen by the user. Because oj04fd counts a pixel change 'inside the scrolling area of the viewport' and never requires the user to be able to see it without manual scrolling — and the corpus places every indicator immediately adjacent in
scenario: Online-banking 'Recent transactions' card with overflow:hidden; each row's round details button is pinned flush to (and slightly past) the card's right edge via transform:translateX(13px), so its focus ring is a circle whose right half is clipped off the card by the ancestor's overflow:hidden — only a meaningless left crescent survives.
mechanism: Focus ring is drawn (3px outline + 3px offset) but the focusable .row .go button straddles the .card{overflow:hidden} boundary, so the right half of the ring is painted outside the clip box and removed; verified in Chromium with ring-visible fraction ~0.55 and the right rail clipped.
